About: Twin Paradox · Worldline Comparison

Source

Lecture
12 — Twin paradox
Simulation
Simulation 1 — Twin paradox worldline comparison (guided inquiry)
Concept
The twin on the straight (inertial) worldline between two events always accumulates the most proper time — no single inertial frame keeps the travelling twin at rest for the whole journey.
Serves
Analyse the twin paradox with spacetime diagrams; distinguish inertial vs non-inertial motion; explain the role of acceleration without making it the direct cause; resolve apparent paradoxes via proper time.
Inquiry
Step 1 — predict who ages more. Step 2 — read the proper times and compare across frames. Step 3 — find whether any single inertial frame keeps Bella at rest, and what physical event breaks the symmetry.
Misconception
"It's symmetric — from Bella's view Alice travels away and comes back, so they age the same." (Encoded as prediction choice (c) and the Step-3 friend persona.)

Twin Paradox
Two worldlines joining the same pair of events — one straight, one bent at a turnaround.

Welcome toTwin paradox

Two twins part at one event and meet again at another — what do their clocks read?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

Guided Inquiry

1 · Two twins, two worldlines

Let’s set the scene. Alice stays at x = 0 while Bella flies out at speed v, turns around at Eₜ, and comes back. Both twins leave the event E₁ and meet again at E₂. Each twin’s own clock measures the proper time τ along her own worldline — τA along Alice’s straight path, τB along Bella’s bent one.

2 · Predict

Let’s start with the classic question. Bella departs at v = 0.60c, turns around at E₍ₜ₎, and returns at the same speed. At the reunion E₂, which twin do you think has aged more?

The τ counters beside each dot are live now. Let the sweep run all the way to E₂ and watch them separate.

3 · Push the turnaround out

Now let’s push things further. Raise v and Bella’s turnaround swings further out in space, while E₁ and E₂ stay where they are. Her drawn path on the page gets longer. So what do you think happens to τB?

Go ahead and slide the speed v: the turnaround swings wider, Bella’s path grows on the page, and τB falls.

4 · The symmetry claim

A friend says:
“From Bella’s point of view, Alice travels away and comes back, so they must age the same.”

Your friend’s point is worth taking seriously. Both worldlines join E₁ to E₂. So what makes the two twins non-interchangeable?

Try each reference frame in turn: Alice’s worldline is one straight segment in all of them, and Bella’s corner at Eₜ never disappears.

5 · A second observer

One last test. A second observer flies past at speed v and redraws both worldlines, so every event’s coordinates change. Which quantities do you think that observer reads the same as we do?

Switch to Bella’s outbound frame (S′) and watch: the “now” line’s t′ runs to a different total while τA and τB hold.

6 · Maximal ageing

Here’s the whole story in a nutshell. Between two timelike-separated events, the straight, inertial worldline records the greatest proper time. Bella returns younger not because anything happened to her body, but because her worldline is bent — and in Minkowski geometry a bend costs proper time: Δτ = √(−Δs²), and every sideways step pushes Δs² = −Δt² + Δx² towards zero. And the proper time each twin carries is the same number in every frame.

Twin Paradox

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Two twins leave the same event and meet again at the same later event, each carrying a clock. This sim draws both journeys on a spacetime diagram and counts each clock's proper time, so you can compare what the two clocks read when the twins meet.

What you'll learn

  • How a clock's reading follows from the path it travels through spacetime.
  • How Bella's clock total depends on her speed v.
  • What a change of reference frame does to each reading.
  • What a light signal from Bella tells Alice, and when.
Both twins leave E₁ and meet at E₂. Alice stays at x = 0. Bella turns around at Eₜ.

What's on screen

  • Alice's worldline (blue): a straight line up x = 0.
  • Bella's worldline (red): out at speed v to the turnaround Eₜ, then back to E₂.
  • "Now" line (dashed amber): sweeps up once, through the events that are simultaneous in the frame shown. A dot marks where it crosses each worldline, with a τ counter: that twin's proper time so far.
  • Readings panel: the totals, and the numbers for the frame you are viewing.
See itRun one sweep in Alice's frame. Watch for: the dashed "now" line climbing, with a dot on each worldline where it crosses.

03

Proper time is what a clock reads along its own path

A worldline is a twin's path through spacetime. A clock carried along it records the proper time τ. With c = 1, a straight stretch that covers Δt in time and Δx in distance has interval Δs² = −Δt² + Δx² and proper time Δτ = √(−Δs²). A bent path is a sum of straight pieces; a smooth one is an integral:

Proper time along a worldline from E₁ to E₂, with ds² = −dt² + dx².

Alice stays at x = 0, so Δx = 0 and her clock simply counts the coordinate time. From E₁ to E₂ that is T = 10 yr.

The interval is Δs² = −c²Δt² + Δx², so a timelike pair has Δs² < 0 and its proper time is Δτ = √(−Δs²)/c.

Key idea. Each clock reads the length of its own worldline, measured with this rule. Two clocks that travel different paths between the same two events need not read the same total.
See itRun one sweep in Alice's frame. Watch for: the counter beside Alice's dot always matching the "now" line's time, while Bella's counter reads less.
04

Bella's two legs add up to less than Alice's one

Each of Bella's legs lasts Δt = T/2 and covers Δx = vT/2, so each is worth (T/2)√(1 − v²) of proper time. Together:

The totals at E₂. γ is the same factor that appears in time dilation.

Her path looks longer on the page, but in Δs² = −Δt² + Δx² sideways distance pushes Δs² towards zero, and Δτ = √(−Δs²) falls with it. The faster she goes, the further out Eₜ swings and the less her clock records.

Three of Bella's journeys between the same E₁ and E₂, against Alice's.
v

This slider moves the sim's speed control too.

The gap grows slowly at first and then quickly. At v = 0.10c it is only 0.05 yr (about 18 days); at v = 0.80c it is a full 4.00 yr.

See itPush v to the top of its range. Watch for: the turnaround Eₜ swinging out while τB falls.
05

The bend is what separates the twins

Between two events, the straight, inertial worldline records the greatest proper time. Any bend between them lowers it.

  • Alice is inertial from E₁ to E₂: one straight line, one inertial frame (S).
  • Bella needs two inertial frames, S′ on the way out and S″ on the way back, and she switches between them at Eₜ.
  • The bend belongs to her worldline, not to a frame. Redraw the picture in S, S′ or S″ and the corner at Eₜ is still there.
  • The turnaround is instantaneous in this sim, and T√(1 − v²) has no acceleration term in it. The result comes from the shape of the path.
Key idea. The two twins are not interchangeable: only one worldline bends. Looking from Bella's side does not straighten it.
See itView the trip from Bella's frame for the whole journey. Watch for: around the halfway point of the sweep, a pulsing ring at Eₜ labelled "turnaround — Bella switches frames".
06

A change of frame changes t and x, not τ

The sim's two boosts (c = 1) relabel every event:

S′ holds Bella at rest on the way out; S″ holds her at rest on the way back.
  • In S′, Bella is at rest on the way out and Alice moves at −v. Bella's return leg is faster there, with speed w, still below c:
  • The reunion E₂ lands at t′ = γT, which is 12.50 yr at v = 0.60c, at x′ = −γvT. That is a coordinate time in S′, not the reading of either twin's clock.
  • Alice's clock still reads τA = 10.00 yr and Bella's τB = 8.00 yr (at v = 0.60c). A boost preserves Δs² = −Δt² + Δx² along every piece of every worldline, so each total keeps its value.
See itView the trip from Bella's outbound frame. Watch for: the "now" time running past 10 yr toward γT, while the τ totals stay as they were.
07

Without a reunion, "at the same time" depends on the frame

In One-way + signal mode Bella never turns around. At Esend (t = T/2 in S) she radios Alice, and the light signal reaches Alice at Erecv. At v = 0.60c:

quantityformulavalue
Bella's clock when she signals(T/2)/γ4.00 yr
Where she is, in SvT/23.00 ly
Alice's clock when it arrives(T/2)(1 + v)8.00 yr

Ask what Alice's clock read at the moment Bella signalled. In S the answer is 5.00 yr. In S′ it is (T/2)/γ² = 3.20 yr. The two frames draw different "now" lines through Esend, and they meet Alice's worldline at different events. There is no second shared event, so there is no frame-free answer.

Key idea. "Alice's age at the moment of the signal" depends on the frame. The 8.00 yr she reads when the signal arrives does not, because that reading is an event at her own clock.
See itPause the "now" line at Bella's signal event, first in S and then in S′. Watch for: Alice's clock at the signal reading 5.00 yr in S, then 3.20 yr in S′ (at v = 0.60c).
08

Where it matters

  • Cosmic-ray muons. At rest a muon lasts 2.2 μs on average, enough to travel about 0.66 km. Take one made 15 km up at 0.994c: the trip takes about 50 μs by Earth clocks but only 5.5 μs by its own, about 2.5 lifetimes. That is why a useful fraction reach the ground.
  • GPS. The satellites move at about 3.9 km/s, so speed alone slows their clocks by about 7 μs a day. Gravity, which this sim does not model, speeds them up by about 46 μs a day. Without a correction for both, position errors would grow by about 11 km a day.
  • Muon storage rings. At CERN in 1977, muons circling at γ ≈ 29 lived about 64 μs instead of 2.2 μs. They were accelerating all the time, yet the lifetime matched the prediction from their speed alone.
Go deeper: any path, not just two straight legs
  • For a worldline with speed u(t) = dx/dt below c, τ = ∫√(1 − u²) dt. In Alice's frame the integrand is 1 for her and below 1 whenever Bella moves, so no path from E₁ to E₂ beats Alice's.
  • A turn that takes a short time changes τB only slightly. The sim's sharp corner is the limit of a quick turn.
09

Summary

In one line. A clock reads the proper time along its own worldline. Alice's straight path from E₁ to E₂ records T, Bella's bent one records T√(1 − v²), and every frame agrees on both totals.

Key points

  • Proper time is Δτ = √(−Δs²), with Δs² = −Δt² + Δx² and c = 1, added up along the worldline.
  • τB = T/γ falls as v rises, though her drawn path gets longer.
  • Only Bella's worldline bends. A boost changes t and x but not τ, and "at the same time" depends on the frame.

Common mix-ups

  • "Bella sees Alice moving, so the two twins are symmetric." Alice's worldline is straight in every frame. Bella's bend never disappears, and only she changes inertial frame.
  • "A longer path on the page means more time for Bella." That is the Euclidean instinct. In Δs² = −Δt² + Δx² the spatial step has the opposite sign to the time step, so it lowers the proper time Δτ = √(−Δs²).
  • "The acceleration at the turnaround is what slows her clock." The result T√(1 − v²) contains no acceleration. It comes from the shape of her path.

Things to try on your own

  • Set v = 0.80c and check τB in the Readings panel against T√(1 − 0.80²).
  • View S′ at v = 0.50c and compare Bella's return speed on the diagram with 2v/(1 + v²).
  • In One-way mode at v = 0.30c, work out τB and the arrival time before you read them off.
